//* SET, EXEC PARM. / COND. overrides of a PROC step, a DD override, a
//* DD added to a PROC step, INCLUDE, JCLLIB ORDER) and
//* stepname.procstepname tests inside IF. The resolved step lists
//* and the run / bypass answers are in scenarios.json, written from
//* IBM's z/OS MVS JCL Reference (SA23-1385) before any evaluator ran
//* on them. Library members: "libraries" in scenarios.json.
resolve_input: resolve: the call step of a job, e.g. S1 of SYMJOB; libraries are the libraries object of this file.
resolve_answer: expect: per proc step (key CALLSTEP.PROCSTEP, or CALLSTEP for a plain step), pgm; parm and cond only where the scenario is about them; dd = every DD naming a DSN, in the order the step ends up with them, as {ddname: dsn}.
flow_input: given: per step that starts, {rc: n} or {abend: code}, keyed by CALLSTEP.PROCSTEP for a procedure's step.
flow_answer: expect: per step in execution order, run or bypass.

resolve.basis: Symbolic parameters, PROC statement: a value coded on the PROC statement is the default and is used when the calling EXEC assigns none. &HLQ..IN.&SUF: the first period ends the symbolic name, the second is the literal period, so PROD.IN.DATA; the PARM operand's quotes do not stop substitution of &PRM.

A value assigned on the calling EXEC overrides the PROC statement default, in every procedure statement that names the symbolic, steps P1 and P2 alike. SUF is not assigned, so its default DATA stands.
EXEC PROC=CATP is the keyword form of EXEC CATP. Only SUF is assigned; HLQ and PRM keep their PROC statement defaults.
SET statement: it assigns a value to a symbolic parameter used in the JCL statements that follow it, up to the next SET of the same name.
SET statement: the second SET of QUAL replaces the first for the statements after it; D1 above keeps PAYR.
A call that overrides nothing resolves to the procedure's statements as written.

EXEC PARM.procstepname= and COND.procstepname= replace the PARM and COND on that procedure step only; the new COND replaces the old one, it does not add a test (so (4,LT,A1) is gone). A1 is not named, so it keeps PARM X1 and has no COND.

DD statement in a calling job, procstepname.ddname form: it overrides the procedure step's DD of that name (the DSN is replaced, A1's other DD SYSUT2 is untouched). A DD whose ddname the procedure step lacks (A2.EXTRA) is added to that step, after the procedure's own DDs; overrides precede added DDs and follow the order of the procedure's steps.
JCLLIB statement: the system searches the libraries in ORDER, in the order coded; PRC1 is in both LIB.A and LIB.B and the first library, LIB.A, supplies it.
JCLLIB statement: a member absent from the first library is looked for in the next; PRC2 is only in LIB.B.
As jcllib-first-library-wins with ORDER=(LIB.B,LIB.A): the same member now comes from LIB.B.

JCL Reference, 'Using a procedure' (p. 26): the system retrieves a called procedure from the job input stream first, then from the private libraries of the JCLLIB statement. PRC3 is both an in-stream procedure and in LIB.A: the in-stream one is used.
LIBJOB2 has no in-stream PRC3, so the search reaches LIB.A (the second library) and finds it.

INCLUDE statement: the statements of the member replace the INCLUDE, so the member's DD belongs to the step above. JCLLIB ORDER (p. 380): 'The system searches the libraries in the order in which you specify them'; INCLUDE groups are searched in the same order as procedures ('Considerations for using INCLUDE groups', p. 376).
As include-group-first-library with ORDER=(LIB.B,LIB.A).

JCL Reference, EXEC PARM, 'On an EXEC statement that calls a procedure' (p. 353) and Example 2: PARM without procstepname overrides the PARM on the first EXEC statement only and the system nullifies the PARM on any following EXEC statement in the procedure. Chapter 5 'Modifying EXEC statement parameters' (p. 29) repeats it. COND is not coded on the call, so each step keeps its own.

JCL Reference, EXEC COND, 'On an EXEC statement that calls a procedure' (p. 345): the COND on the calling EXEC overrides the COND on a called EXEC (B2's (4,LT,B1) is replaced, not joined) and is added to a called EXEC that has none (B1, B3); with no procstepname it applies to all steps of the procedure. The PARMs are not touched.

JCL Reference, 'Defining and nullifying JCL symbols' (pp. 39-40) and 'Using symbols in nested procedures' rule 4 with Table 13 (pp. 51-52): a SET value is used for a symbol in a procedure only when the calling EXEC and the PROC statement do not also define it. A has a PROC default, so it is PROCA, not SETA; B is on the PROC statement only; Q has no EXEC or PROC value, so SETQ. In &C..F3 the first period ends the name and is consumed.

JCL Reference, 'Defining and nullifying JCL symbols' (pp. 39-40, 42): an EXEC value overrides the PROC default (A=EXECA, over PROCA and over SETA); C= on the EXEC nullifies the symbol, and 'if you use an EXEC statement to nullify a JCL symbol, and a PROC statement specifies a default, the JCL symbol is nullified' (p. 42), so &C.. gives the empty text and the DSN is HLQ.F3.

JCL Reference, 'Nested procedures' and 'Examples of modifying nested procedures', Example 1 (pp. 32-34): procedure A calls B calls C and the manual lists the statements the job stream is equivalent to: CS1 (level 3), BS2 (level 2), AS2 (level 1). B's CS1.CS1DD1 overrides C's DD (A.B.C becomes X.Y.Z), A's BS2.BS2DD2 adds a DD to B's step BS2 and the job's AS2.AS2DD2 adds one to A's step AS2, each after the DDs the step already had. CS1DD2 and CS1DD3 are SYSOUT DDs and name no DSN.

JCL Reference, 'Using symbols in nested procedures' rules 2-5, Table 13 and its Example 1 (pp. 47-49): STEP1 nullifies A and sets C=789, B stays 456 from the SET (level 1: A=,B=456,C=789); PSTEP1 sets A=ABC,B=DEF for PROC2 (level 2: A=ABC,B=DEF,C=789), so SYSUT1 is ABC.DEF; the manual's own listing shows the level-1 values coming back after PROC2, so PSTEP2's P2DD (X&A..&B..&C, the first period of each pair ends the name) is X.456.789. P2STEP1's SYSOUT DDs name no DSN. The level-0 step BARNEY sees A=123,B=456 (checked in nested-symbols-level-zero).
Same example (p. 49): after the nested expansion 'the substitution texts for symbols are restored to their original values: A=123,B=456', so BD DSN=Z&A..&B is Z123.456.

JCL Reference, 'Additional rules for modifying DD parameters' (p. 29) and DD DSNAME / DUMMY (NULLFILE 'has the same effect as coding the DD DUMMY parameter'): K1.D1 DUMMY nullifies the DSN of D1; K1.D2 DSN=NULLFILE is a dummy too; K1.D3 DSN=NEW.D3, 'a name other than NULLFILE', nullifies D3's DUMMY, so D3 names NEW.D3 in D3's own place; D7 is DSN=NULLFILE in the procedure (a dummy) and K1.D7 DSN=NEW.D7 replaces it. D4 is SYSOUT and names no DSN; D5 is untouched. Order: the procedure's DD order.
Same pages: with no override D3 (DUMMY), D4 (SYSOUT) and D7 (DSN=NULLFILE) name no data set.
DD DUMMY (p. 12920 of the V3R1 text, 'Overriding a procedure DD statement'): an overriding SYSOUT parameter with a subparameter value nullifies the DUMMY; the DD is then a sysout DD and names no DSN.

JCL Reference, INCLUDE statement, 'Location in the JCL' and 'Considerations for using INCLUDE groups' (Chapter 19): an INCLUDE may appear anywhere after the JOB statement and after JCLLIB, must follow a complete statement, and 'can appear within an INCLUDE group' (up to 15 levels); the group replaces the statement. Here OUTER (an INCLUDE of STDDDS, then OUTA) sits in step N1 of the procedure after N1DD, so N1 ends with N1DD, INCA (from STDDDS), OUTA; N2 gets none. Groups are searched like procedures, along ORDER (p. 376): LIB.A first.
Same, ORDER=(LIB.B,LIB.A): OUTER exists only in LIB.A, but its inner INCLUDE of STDDDS is searched along ORDER again and LIB.B holds a STDDDS, so the DD is INCB.

JCL Reference, 'Defining and nullifying JCL symbols' (p. 36-37): 'If you specify duplicate JCL symbols on a PROC statement, the system uses the first substitution text as the default.' PROC DP codes Q=FIRST,Q=SECOND and E1 supplies no Q: FIRST.
Same section (p. 36): 'If you specify duplicate JCL symbols on an EXEC statement, the system uses the first substitution text as the default.' E2 codes Q=XA,Q=XB over the PROC default: XA.
Same section (p. 37): 'If you define duplicate JCL symbols on a SET statement, the system assigns the last substitution text to the JCL symbol.' SET Z=ONE,Z=TWO: TWO.

INCLUDE statement (p. 376): a group may hold DD and OUTPUT JCL statements (the manual's own example 1, member SYSOUT2: a SYSOUT DD and three OUTPUT statements). The SYSOUT DD names no data set and OUTPUT statements are not DDs, so O1 ends with its own DD only.

INCLUDE statement, 'Considerations for using INCLUDE groups' (p. 376): values assigned to symbolic parameters in an INCLUDE group (such as with SET) are valid for use on subsequent JCL statements, so a statement coded before the INCLUDE still sees the job's SET: BEFORE.DATA.
Same section (p. 376): the group replaces the INCLUDE statement, and 'You can put EXEC statements' in it; the SET on its first line holds for the statements after it, so X2's DD is FROMGRP.DATA.

Same section (p. 376): 'you can put EXEC statements that invoke procedures in an INCLUDE group', and an INCLUDE group can hold INCLUDE statements. GRPX includes GRPY, whose EXEC calls PRC4; PRC4 is found in LIB.A along ORDER and has the one step M1 (PGM=ONLYA).
Same section (p. 376): the SET inside the group is valid for subsequent JCL statements, so X3 after the INCLUDE reads Z as FROMGRP.

SET statement, Purpose (p. 559), and 'Using symbols in nested procedures' rule 4 (p. 48): a SET's value is used in all subsequent statements, and a cataloged procedure may contain SET ('Cataloged procedures', p. 25). TAG is assigned only once inside PSP, neither the PROC statement nor the EXEC assigns it, so D1 (before the SET) reads the outer value OUTER, and D2 and D3 (after it) read INNER.

'Using symbols in nested procedures' rule 4 (p. 48): the SET value is used in 'subsequent statements, procedures, and nested procedures'; rule 5: a symbol the inner procedure does not assign takes its value from the procedure it is nested in. PSO's SET gives NEST=FROMOUT, PSI assigns none, so R1D is FROMOUT.R.

'Examples of coding symbols in nested procedures', Example 1 (pp. 48-49): when a procedure's expansion is complete the values return to those held before it, and at level 0 (BARNEY) the substitution texts are restored. PSP's SET TAG=INNER is gone by C3, which reads the level-0 SET, OUTER.

INCLUDE statement (pp. 375-376): the group replaces the INCLUDE statement and its statements are processed as part of the JCL stream; a cataloged procedure may contain INCLUDE and SET (p. 25); a group may hold EXEC statements (also ones that invoke procedures) and nested INCLUDEs; a SET in a group is valid for subsequent statements. So PIG's steps are A1, then the group's G1 (GT=FROMGRP), then GRPY's call of PRC4 (member of LIB.A, one step M1, ONLYA), then A2 reading GT as FROMGRP.

flow.basis: IF relational expression, stepname.procstepname.RC: R1.Q1.RC = 0 and R1.Q2.RC <= 4 are both true, so the THEN clause R2 runs and R3 (ELSE) does not. R1.Q2.RUN = TRUE: Q2 ran. ABENDCC = S0C7: nothing abended, false. R6 COND (4,LT,R1.Q2): 4 < 0 false, runs.
Q2's own COND (4,LT,Q1): 4 < 0 false, Q2 runs. R1.Q2.RC <= 4 is false, so the ELSE clause R3 runs. R6 COND (4,LT,R1.Q2): 4 < 8, bypass.

Q2's COND (4,LT,Q1): 4 < 8 true, Q2 is bypassed. R1.Q1.RC = 0 false, so R3. R1.Q2.RUN = TRUE: Q2 did not run, false, so R4 is bypassed. R6: the COND test names a bypassed step, which is false (IBM: a bypassed step tests false), so R6 runs.

Q2 has no EVEN / ONLY, so it is bypassed after the abend. R1.Q1.ABENDCC = S0C7 is true, R5 runs. R6 has no EVEN / ONLY, bypassed. ASSUMED A3 (as ifelse A3): the two IFs that do not name ABEND or ABENDCC are not evaluated after an abend, so R2, R3 and R4 start nothing.
As ifp-q1-abends-s0c7, but R1.Q1.ABENDCC = S0C7 is false for S806, so R5 is bypassed too.

PRC4 is a library member (JCLLIB ORDER=(LIB.B,LIB.A); first library holding it wins (JCLLIB ORDER, p. 380), so LIB.B's two-step PRC4, not LIB.A's one-step one). Its steps are addressed T1.M1 / T1.M2 exactly as an in-stream procedure's. M1 rc 0: M2 COND (4,LT,M1) is 4 < 0, false, so M2 runs. T1.M2.RC = 0 is true, T2 runs, ELSE T3 does not. T1.M2.RUN = FALSE is false (M2 ran), T4 is bypassed. T5 COND (4,LT,T1.M1): 4 < 0 false, runs.

M1 ends rc 8: M2 COND (4,LT,M1) is 4 < 8, true, so M2 is bypassed. A bypassed step has no return code, so T1.M2.RC = 0 is false and ELSE T3 runs; T1.M2.RUN = FALSE is true (M2 did not run), T4 runs. T5 COND (4,LT,T1.M1) is 4 < 8, true, bypassed.

assumed.text: After an ordinary abend an IF construct that does not name ABEND or ABENDCC starts nothing (same as tests/equivalence/jcl/ifelse A3).

A step of a nested procedure is answered under the key CALLSTEP.PROCSTEP naming the PGM step itself (the manual's 'equivalent statements' flatten the levels and give only PGM steps; stepname.procstepname in IF and COND is documented for a step with PGM, not a path through levels).

refused.construct: unqualified PARM= or COND= together with the PARM.procstep= / COND.procstep= form on one call
refused.why: the manual states each form alone (pp. 345, 353) and is silent on their combination

refused.construct: a SYSOUT, * or DATA override of a DD that names a DSN
refused.why: the manual lets DSNAME be coded with SYSOUT (to name the sysout data set) and does not say the overridden DSN is nullified, so the DD may or may not still name it (read again 2026-11-19: 'Modifying procedures' p. 27-28 makes only a mutually exclusive parameter nullify the overridden one, and DSNAME is coded with SYSOUT or DD * to name the data set, so the two are not mutually exclusive: no answer)

refused.construct: a backward reference (procstepname.procstepname.ddname) or a modifying statement addressed to a step the procedure does not hold or to a step that itself calls a procedure
refused.why: 'Modifying nested procedures' rules 3 and 5 (p. 33) call them invalid and the example (p. 34) marks them JCL errors

refused.construct: EXEC PARM= or COND= on a call of a procedure that itself calls procedures, PARM.procstep= / COND.procstep= naming a calling step
refused.why: the manual does not say which nested step the unqualified form reaches

refused.construct: nested procedure calls evaluated in IF flow (expand_flow_rows)
refused.why: the manual defines stepname.procstepname for a step with PGM, not a path through nested levels

refused.construct: an in-stream procedure coded after the EXEC that calls it
refused.why: the manual says it must be placed before (p. 26) and does not say whether the library member is then used or the job fails

refused.construct: a SET inside a procedure for a symbol that the calling EXEC or the PROC statement also assigns
refused.why: 'Using symbols in nested procedures' rule 4 (p. 48) says such a symbol applies 'only to subsequent statements within that PROC', while the SET statement chapter (p. 559) says values assigned by the calling EXEC or PROC statements override the SET values: the two readings differ and the manual does not reconcile them

refused.construct: a SET inside a procedure whose value holds a symbol (SET Z=&Y)
refused.why: the INCLUDE chapter (p. 376) says values current when a symbol is encountered are substituted, but the manual gives no example of a SET value that itself holds a symbol inside a procedure, so the resolver does not carry it

invalid.why: 'Nested procedures' (p. 32): up to 15 levels; a step at level 15 is allowed, a call from level 15 is not. Raised as JclProcRefused naming 15 levels
INCLUDE statement, 'Location in the JCL' (p. 376): nested up to a maximum of 15 levels

invalid.construct: an INCLUDE group holding a JOB, PROC, PEND or JCLLIB statement (or JES2 / JES3 statements)
invalid.why: 'Considerations for using INCLUDE groups' (p. 376) lists them as not allowed
'Rules for defining JCL symbols' (p. 37): all JCL symbols coded in the JCL must have defined values
